reader.title: Reported lynching of horse thieves in the Cimarron district (1888)
bases: The only reports describe settlers 'making war' on horse thieves and a rumor that thirteen had been lynched (A1, A2).

The dispatch passes on an unconfirmed report that thirteen men had been lynched, and says its bearers 'could give nothing definite'; no victim, place, perpetrator or confirmation appears in the coverage (A1, A2).
All three items reprint one Clayton, N.M., wire dispatch word for word, and that dispatch itself relays an unverified report (A1, A2, A3).

summary.text: The reported lynching of horse thieves in the Cimarron district was an unconfirmed report, carried in a wire dispatch from Clayton, New Mexico, dated July 5, 1888, that settlers had lynched thirteen horse thieves on the night of Monday, July 2.
The dispatch itself said the men who brought the report "could give nothing definite," and no confirmation, names or follow-up appear in the coverage.
Papers in Dakota and Minnesota nonetheless ran it under headlines stating that settlers had "strung up" eleven horse thieves.
According to the Clayton dispatch, the "Cimmaron district" was "infested with horse-thieves," and the settlers there were "beginning to make war on them."
The dispatch did not say in which state or territory the district lay, and one paper's headline called the area "Lawless No Man's Land."
The only account of the killings is secondhand: a report "was brought in" to Clayton that thirteen men had been lynched on Monday night.
No victims were named, no place or method was described, and the dispatch attributed the war on the thieves only to "the settlers."
No report of an inquest, arrest or later confirmation was found.
The story reached print only as a brief wire item in papers in Dakota and Minnesota.
The Wahpeton Times ran it on July 5 at the head of a crime column titled "LAWLESS NO MAN'S LAND," whose deck said settlers had strung up eleven horse thieves "as a Slight Warning."
The Dickinson Press on July 7 and the Morris Tribune on July 11 printed the same text under "Strung Up Eleven Horse Thieves."
In each case the headline presented as a completed act, and with a different number, what the dispatch itself called an indefinite report.
None of the papers commented on the killings or questioned them.
The number of men said to have been lynched differs within the same items: the dispatch text gave thirteen, while the editors' headlines gave eleven.
Neither figure was confirmed, since the dispatch stressed that the report's bearers had nothing definite to offer.

accounts.label: Clayton, N.M., wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Settlers in the horse-thief-infested Cimarron district had begun making war on the thieves; a report came in that thirteen were lynched Monday night, but its bearers could give nothing definite.

accounts.label: Headline writers
accounts.gist: The headlines turned the rumor into a completed act and gave a different number: settlers 'String Up Eleven' horse thieves, in one paper 'as a Slight Warning'.

framing.detail: The Wahpeton Times headed it 'LAWLESS NO MAN'S LAND' and said settlers strung up eleven 'as a Slight Warning', in a column of crime news.
The Dickinson Press and Morris Tribune ran the same dispatch under 'Strung Up Eleven Horse Thieves', with no comment.

versions.value: thirteen (dispatch text, as an unconfirmed report)

conflicts.note: The same item gives both numbers; the text is the dispatch's own wording, the headline was added by the editors and states as fact what the text calls indefinite.
